frictionVectors.title: EU energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria is using pipeline and LNG exports to preserve bargaining power with Europe while resisting deeper foreign control of upstream assets. Contract terms and political disputes periodically complicate investment.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel and Morocco pressure
frictionVectors.details: Instability across the Sahel and strategic rivalry with Morocco increase security costs and complicate Algeria's regional infrastructure and diplomatic posture.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Angola retains formal control over petroleum resources but remains exposed to foreign oil companies, lenders, and commodity-price volatility. Debt-linked infrastructure arrangements continue to constrain policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito corridor geopolitics
frictionVectors.details: The corridor is attracting U.S., European, and Chinese interest because of its access to Central African copper and cobalt. Competition brings investment but raises concerns over transit rights, strategic dependence, and local value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Niger pipeline confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The Niger-Benin oil export route remains vulnerable to political friction after Niger's military takeover and bilateral tensions. Border restrictions and diplomatic disputes can reduce throughput and weaken Benin's projected transit revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Port and security exposure
frictionVectors.details: Cotonou's expansion increases Benin's economic leverage but also deepens reliance on external financiers, operators, and regional trade flows. Sahelian militant spillover threatens northern transport and investment corridors.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is pressing for a larger domestic share of diamond value and greater marketing autonomy. The strategy strengthens sovereignty but faces pressure from weak global diamond demand and the country's dependence on the sector.

frictionVectors.title: Water and energy constraints
frictionVectors.details: Mining expansion and urban growth are constrained by scarce water, imported energy, and limited domestic infrastructure. New mineral projects could increase external leverage unless processing capacity develops locally.

frictionVectors.title: Mining contract nationalism
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater state participation, local processing, and tighter oversight of gold operations while reducing reliance on Western mining partners. Administrative and security weaknesses make implementation uneven.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security alignment
frictionVectors.details: Closer ties with Russian security actors provide an alternative to former Western partnerships but may create opaque financial, mining, and infrastructure arrangements. Insurgent attacks continue to threaten mines, roads, and state revenue collection.

highlights: Mining Opening Under Tight State Control
Rwanda Ties Remain a Security Fault Line

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Mineral Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking foreign capital for nickel, gold, and rare-earth development while struggling to secure transparent terms and domestic value addition. External financing needs limit the government's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Border Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Rwanda remain strained over armed-group allegations and border security. Instability in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo continues to expose Burundi to spillover and competing regional influence.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Competition
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde is using its ports, air links, and maritime position to attract European, North American, and Gulf investment. The main sovereignty risk is dependence on external capital for strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and Energy Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains vulnerable to externally driven tourism cycles, imported fuel costs, and climate stress. Renewable-energy expansion could improve resilience but still requires foreign finance and technology.

highlights: Resource Base Undercut by Security Fragmentation

frictionVectors.title: Oil, Gas, and Mining Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Cameroon retains formal control over hydrocarbons, timber, and mining assets, but financing, technology, and infrastructure partnerships give foreign firms substantial leverage. Local processing and revenue transparency remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone and Far-North Conflicts
frictionVectors.details: The Anglophone insurgency and Boko Haram-linked violence constrain transport corridors and state access to productive regions. Security dependence and emergency spending divert resources from sovereign development priorities.

highlights: Security Partnership Trades Access for Protection

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security and Mining Linkages
frictionVectors.details: The government's reliance on Russian security personnel has strengthened regime protection but raised concerns that security assistance is tied to privileged access to gold and diamond networks. This weakens transparency and state-wide control over resources.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor and Border Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Most external trade depends on vulnerable routes through Cameroon and neighboring states. Armed groups, weak institutions, and regional competition limit the government's ability to regulate extraction and infrastructure on sovereign terms.

highlights: Oil Revenues Anchor a Fragile State

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Oil Revenue Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad's fiscal sovereignty remains tied to oil production, export infrastructure, and external operators. Volatile prices, limited refining capacity, and weak oversight reduce the developmental value of the resource base.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan Spillover and Security Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: The war in Sudan is increasing refugee, arms, and cross-border militia pressures in eastern Chad. N'Djamena must balance ties with neighboring powers and external security partners while preserving control over strategic territory.

frictionVectors.title: FRANCE–MAYOTTE DISPUTE
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, constraining Comoros' territorial claims and access to surrounding maritime resources. The dispute remains a persistent source of diplomatic friction.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL FINANCING DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on remittances and external partners for infrastructure and budget support, limiting room for autonomous resource and development policy.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONTRACT COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms retain major positions in copper and cobalt, while Western actors seek greater access to critical-mineral supply chains. Contract renegotiation and local-value demands remain central sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: EASTERN SECURITY CRISIS
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving M23 and regional actors continues to undermine state control over territory and mineral corridors. External security and diplomatic involvement is substantial but has not eliminated illicit extraction.

frictionVectors.title: OIL-SECTOR DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenues dominate fiscal capacity, exposing the state to price volatility and limiting diversification. Foreign operators retain significant technical and commercial leverage.

frictionVectors.title: DEBT-FOR-INFRASTRUCTURE EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed infrastructure and creditor relationships remain influential around transport and energy projects. These ties can narrow fiscal policy space and complicate control over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: COCOA VALUE-CHAIN DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Cote d'Ivoire retains limited control over downstream processing, pricing, and global market access despite its producer scale. Foreign traders and processors continue to capture substantial value.

frictionVectors.title: SAHEL SECURITY SPILLOVER
frictionVectors.details: Instability from Burkina Faso and Mali pressures northern border infrastructure and defense spending. International security partnerships support resilience but also increase external operational influence.

highlights: Red Sea position raises strategic leverage

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND DEBT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti's port economy and major infrastructure are closely tied to external financiers and operators, especially China. Debt exposure and revenue concentration constrain autonomous economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: BASES AND REGIONAL RIVALRY
frictionVectors.details: US, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military presences give Djibouti substantial rent income but expose it to great-power competition. Red Sea and Gulf tensions increase pressure on its strategic neutrality.

highlights: Suez remains a strategic revenue shield
Gulf and IMF financing deepen leverage

frictionVectors.title: Nile Water Security
frictionVectors.details: The GERD dispute with Ethiopia continues to expose Egypt’s dependence on negotiated guarantees for its core water supply. Sudan’s instability further complicates downstream coordination.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing
frictionVectors.details: IMF conditions and Gulf investment provide liquidity but increase outside influence over major assets, exchange-rate policy, and infrastructure priorities.

highlights: Asian and Western firms retain strategic access

frictionVectors.title: Maturing Oil and Gas Fields
frictionVectors.details: Falling mature-field output and limited diversification reduce fiscal autonomy, while foreign technical and investment partners remain important to sustaining production.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque Resource Governance
frictionVectors.details: State control over hydrocarbons is strong formally, but opaque contracting and external operators limit transparency and broad domestic benefit from resource revenues.

highlights: Red Sea geography amplifies strategic value

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Gold, copper, and zinc projects depend heavily on foreign capital and operators, creating persistent concerns over revenue sharing, labor conditions, and sovereign oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Militarization
frictionVectors.details: Regional competition around ports and shipping routes increases pressure on Eritrea to accommodate outside security interests while preserving strict control over its coastline.

highlights: Industrial zones seek greater policy autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Regional Economic Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Trade, electricity, transport links, and investment remain closely tied to South Africa and the Southern African Customs Union, limiting independent economic maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure Financing
frictionVectors.details: Industrial and transport projects rely on external lenders and regional supply chains, creating modest exposure to foreign priorities without a direct loss of state ownership.

highlights: Debt and conflict constrain strategic autonomy

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile Diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: The dam expands Ethiopia’s control over domestic electricity generation but remains a major source of tension with Egypt and Sudan over filling, operations, and downstream guarantees.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Finance
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, Turkish, and Western financing supports transport, energy, and telecommunications, but debt restructuring and investor conditions narrow Addis Ababa’s room for policy independence.

highlights: Manganese and oil remain strategic anchors

frictionVectors.title: French commercial retrenchment
frictionVectors.details: The post-Bongo authorities are renegotiating long-standing French economic and security influence while seeking broader partnerships. This creates uncertainty around oil, mining, logistics, and defense relationships.

frictionVectors.title: Manganese and port concentration
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-linked operators retain substantial influence over manganese extraction and export infrastructure. Limited domestic processing capacity constrains Gabon's ability to capture more value from its mineral base.

highlights: Senegal remains the critical external partner

frictionVectors.title: Senegalese economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for transport links, market access, fuel, and regional security. This dependence supports stability but limits independent control over key corridors and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Coastal fisheries pressure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign industrial fishing and weak enforcement continue to threaten local fishing communities and food security. Fisheries governance remains vulnerable to external commercial interests and limited state capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and gold leakage
frictionVectors.details: Unregulated mining damages water systems, farmland, and public revenues while enabling foreign-linked equipment and trading networks to capture value. Efforts to formalize the sector face entrenched local and transnational interests.

frictionVectors.title: External financing constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and dependence on international financial support limit fiscal autonomy and infrastructure choices. Ghana is balancing creditor demands against pressure to retain greater control over gold, oil, and critical mineral development.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou foreign consortium leverage
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore corridor brings major Chinese and international capital into mining, rail, and port infrastructure. Guinea may gain transformative revenues, but foreign operators retain significant technical, financing, and logistical leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Transition uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Military-led political management weakens predictable institutional oversight of mining contracts and public revenues. Sanctions risk and uncertain civilian transition timelines complicate long-term sovereignty over strategic assets.

highlights: Fragile state control over maritime assets

frictionVectors.title: Transnational narcotics networks
frictionVectors.details: Guinea-Bissau's weak institutions and porous maritime space leave ports, islands, and security services vulnerable to international cocaine trafficking. Trafficking revenues undermine public authority and create openings for foreign coercion.

frictionVectors.title: External dependence in fisheries and infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing interests and donor-backed infrastructure dominate key parts of the coastal economy. Limited enforcement and administrative capacity reduce the state's ability to capture sustainable value from fisheries and ports.

highlights: Ports and minerals face strategic competition

frictionVectors.title: External debt and infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Kenya remains reliant on external creditors, including China and multilateral lenders, while debt-service pressure constrains independent infrastructure and industrial policy.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals governance
frictionVectors.details: New efforts to retain more value from titanium, rare earths, and other minerals are challenged by foreign capital requirements and limited domestic processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water exports to South Africa provide vital revenue but deepen Pretoria's leverage over Lesotho's infrastructure, energy, and fiscal choices.

frictionVectors.title: Political and fiscal fragility
frictionVectors.details: Coalition instability and dependence on external development finance limit the government's ability to negotiate resource projects on fully sovereign terms.

frictionVectors.title: Iron-ore concession dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign-operated mining concessions, particularly around iron ore, provide employment and revenue but leave Liberia exposed to corporate bargaining power and commodity cycles.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics control
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investment dominates key transport and port infrastructure, limiting domestic capture of value from resource exports and regional trade.

frictionVectors.title: Competing control of oil assets
frictionVectors.details: Rival authorities, armed groups, and the National Oil Corporation contest access to fields, terminals, and revenue, leaving production vulnerable to coercion and shutdowns.

frictionVectors.title: Turkish and Russian strategic footholds
frictionVectors.details: Foreign military and commercial networks influence ports, airfields, energy projects, and political bargaining, substantially narrowing Libya's autonomous policy space.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of nickel and cobalt value chains
frictionVectors.details: Large overseas-backed projects dominate nickel, cobalt, and related exports, while Madagascar captures limited downstream value and remains exposed to external price and financing pressures.

frictionVectors.title: Land, water, and environmental conflict
frictionVectors.details: Mining and infrastructure projects face local resistance over land access, water use, and ecological damage, creating openings for foreign firms and donors to shape domestic policy.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt Leverage
frictionVectors.details: IMF-backed reforms and creditor negotiations are narrowing Malawi's policy space, while foreign-exchange shortages constrain fuel, fertilizer, and machinery imports.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Mining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking investment in uranium, rare earths, and niobium, but weak infrastructure and limited domestic processing could leave value capture largely with external firms.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Sector Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is pressing foreign mining companies for higher state participation and revenues, raising contract disputes and operational uncertainty in the gold sector.

frictionVectors.title: Security and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security support has increased, while insecurity threatens transport corridors, mining sites, and access to electricity and fuel.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Gas Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project offers major export revenue but leaves Mauritania dependent on multinational operators, offshore infrastructure, and cross-border coordination with Senegal.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Corridor Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore remains central to the economy, while rail, port, and renewable-energy expansion require substantial external capital and expose the country to commodity and financing shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Implementation Risks
frictionVectors.details: The sovereignty settlement over the Chagos Archipelago strengthens Mauritius's territorial position but leaves unresolved questions over long-term foreign military access and implementation.

frictionVectors.title: Import and Connectivity Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius retains strong institutional control over its economy, yet dependence on imported food, fuel, shipping, and foreign tourism makes it vulnerable to external disruptions.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Contestation
frictionVectors.details: Morocco's control and development of Western Sahara remain contested by Algeria and the Polisario Front, complicating regional security and investment diplomacy.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Desalination, renewables, and hydrogen projects are expanding sovereign capacity, but drought, imported energy inputs, and foreign technology partners remain strategic vulnerabilities.

highlights: Cabo Delgado LNG restart remains pivotal
State control challenged by insurgency and debt

frictionVectors.title: LNG and foreign security dependence
frictionVectors.details: The offshore gas sector is dominated by multinational operators and depends on continued external security support around Cabo Delgado. Delayed production limits Mozambique's fiscal leverage and bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Insurgency and transport corridors
frictionVectors.details: Islamist violence continues to threaten northern communities, logistics routes, and energy infrastructure. Regional and international forces remain important to securing project areas.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of emerging hydrocarbons
frictionVectors.details: Offshore oil discoveries could transform state revenues, but production will require large foreign capital and technical partnerships. Namibia faces pressure to secure stronger local-content and fiscal terms.

frictionVectors.title: Critical minerals and infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Uranium, lithium, port access, and green-hydrogen projects attract competing European, Chinese, and Gulf interests. Limited grid and transport capacity constrains Namibia's ability to capture value domestically.

highlights: Junta asserts control over uranium and oil

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and mining renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The military government is revisiting longstanding French and Western commercial arrangements while seeking greater state control over uranium and other minerals. Political confrontation risks reduced investment and operational disruption.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and border insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Attacks by jihadist groups threaten oil-export infrastructure, roads, and agricultural zones. The withdrawal of regional and Western security partners has increased reliance on alternative external actors.

highlights: Oil reform collides with production insecurity

frictionVectors.title: Oil theft and foreign operator leverage
frictionVectors.details: Pipeline theft, sabotage, and community conflict continue to reduce production and public revenue. International oil companies retain significant technical and financial leverage despite regulatory reforms.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-backed infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, and Western financing supports ports, rail, power, and digital infrastructure, but repayment and concession terms can constrain policy autonomy. Weak domestic power supply limits the sovereign return on these projects.

highlights: Mineral ambitions clash with regional scrutiny
State capacity remains strong but externally pressured

frictionVectors.title: Critical minerals and eastern Congo allegations
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's trading and security links to eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo remain under intense international scrutiny over alleged support for armed groups and mineral flows. Sanctions risk and diplomatic pressure could affect access to finance and markets.

frictionVectors.title: Aid, security, and strategic partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda leverages disciplined institutions and security partnerships to attract investment, but remains sensitive to donor conditionality and reputational pressure. External support is increasingly tied to regional conduct and human-rights concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore exploration dependence
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe remains reliant on foreign capital and technical expertise for prospective offshore blocks. Uncertain discoveries limit immediate leverage but could intensify licensing pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic maritime competition
frictionVectors.details: The archipelago balances Portuguese, Chinese, and wider Gulf of Guinea interests in ports, fisheries, and maritime security. Limited state capacity makes contract transparency and enforcement important sovereignty risks.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and gas contract control
frictionVectors.details: Production from offshore projects gives Dakar greater fiscal room, but foreign operators, lenders, and cost-recovery arrangements will shape how much value remains domestically. Local-content expectations are rising faster than industrial capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Port and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Major transport and energy infrastructure depends on external finance and contractors, including Gulf, European, Chinese, and multilateral partners. Debt discipline and renegotiation risks remain central to preserving policy autonomy.

highlights: Blue economy is the core sovereign asset

frictionVectors.title: Maritime resource protection
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles must protect fisheries and its large maritime zone against illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing with limited surveillance capacity. Partnerships with India, France, and other external actors improve coverage but create coordination sensitivities.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Tourism, port services, and climate-resilience infrastructure remain exposed to external capital and imported systems. The government retains relatively strong institutional control, but concentration among foreign lenders and investors can narrow its options.

highlights: Mining growth tests local value capture
Port access is a strategic battleground

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and mineral dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed iron ore, rutile, and other mining operations dominate the resource-security debate, with disputes over royalties, environmental impacts, and domestic processing. Commodity-price swings and contract renegotiations expose fiscal vulnerability.

frictionVectors.title: 港 infrastructure and logistics influence
frictionVectors.details: Port, road, and mining-corridor projects attract competing Chinese, Middle Eastern, and Western interests. Limited public financing makes infrastructure concessions valuable but increases the risk of opaque terms and uneven national returns.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign security architecture
frictionVectors.details: Somalia depends heavily on external military, financial, and maritime-security support, including Turkish, Gulf, African, and Western partners. Rival partnerships can strengthen the state while also fragmenting command, port access, and strategic decision-making.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore oil and fisheries competition
frictionVectors.details: Prospective offshore hydrocarbons and valuable fisheries attract foreign interest before federal-state arrangements and regulatory capacity are fully settled. Disputes over licensing authority, revenue sharing, and maritime enforcement create significant sovereignty risks.

highlights: Ports and power remain strategic bottlenecks

frictionVectors.title: GRID AND LOGISTICS FRAGILITY
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability and constraints at Transnet's rail network and ports limit sovereign control over mineral exports. Private-sector reforms are advancing, but recovery remains vulnerable to external capital and technical dependence.

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL-MINERALS PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China, and European partners are competing for battery and platinum-group minerals. Pretoria is seeking local beneficiation while resisting alignment with any single external bloc.

frictionVectors.title: SUDAN PIPELINE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's oil exports rely on infrastructure crossing war-affected Sudan, leaving production, transit revenues, and government finances highly vulnerable. Foreign operators and transit authorities retain substantial leverage over the sector.

frictionVectors.title: ELITE CONTROL OF RESOURCE RENT
frictionVectors.details: Oil revenues remain concentrated among political and security elites while fiscal opacity and local conflict undermine public resource sovereignty. International donors and neighboring states continue to shape budgetary and security decisions.

highlights: Gold and ports attract external competition

frictionVectors.title: GOLD SMUGGLING AND WAR FINANCE
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and trafficking provide revenue channels for armed actors and intermediaries, weakening state control over the principal export asset. External buyers and alleged foreign sponsors deepen the fragmentation of the sector.

frictionVectors.title: RED SEA INFRASTRUCTURE CONTEST
frictionVectors.details: Port access, military facilities, and logistics corridors on the Red Sea are increasingly shaped by outside powers seeking strategic footholds. The conflict has reduced Khartoum's ability to negotiate infrastructure terms from a position of sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: LNG PROJECT LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Negotiations with international energy companies over the long-delayed liquefied natural gas project expose Tanzania to investor pressure over fiscal terms, local content, and legal guarantees. Dar es Salaam is seeking greater state participation without deterring capital.

frictionVectors.title: CORRIDOR AND PORT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Dar es Salaam and linked rail corridors are central to regional trade, making Tanzania a target for competing Chinese, Gulf, Turkish, and Western infrastructure interests. Concession terms and debt exposure remain sensitive sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND LOGISTICS INFLUENCE
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's deep-water port gives Togo strategic importance for Sahel trade, but operations and expansion depend heavily on foreign logistics firms and external financing. Regional instability increases both the port's value and its exposure to outside security agendas.

frictionVectors.title: PHOSPHATE VALUE-CHAIN CONSTRAINTS
frictionVectors.details: Togo retains formal ownership of phosphate resources but captures limited value beyond extraction and primary processing. Foreign technology, financing, and market access continue to shape the sector's effective sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: EU MIGRATION AND FINANCE LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: European funding and cooperation remain tied to migration management, giving external partners significant influence over Tunisian policy space.

frictionVectors.title: ENERGY IMPORT VULNERABILITY
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported hydrocarbons and limited investment in domestic generation exposes Tunisia to external price shocks and financing conditions.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP SOVEREIGNTY DISPUTE
frictionVectors.details: The East African Crude Oil Pipeline promises export revenue but leaves Uganda dependent on foreign capital, transit arrangements, and contested environmental safeguards.

frictionVectors.title: CHINESE INFRASTRUCTURE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and contracting remain important to major transport and energy projects, creating long-term repayment and strategic-dependence concerns.

frictionVectors.title: COPPER OWNERSHIP AND VALUE ADDITION
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is pressing for greater fiscal returns and local processing, but its mining sector remains heavily dependent on multinational capital, technology, and export infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: DEBT-LED INFRASTRUCTURE CONSTRAINTS
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and lender conditions limit public investment choices, while transport corridors and power shortages continue to affect mineral sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: MINERAL CONCESSION DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Lithium, platinum, gold, and other mineral projects draw strong Chinese and other foreign interest, while opaque contracting and limited beneficiation can reduce domestic gains.

frictionVectors.title: POWER AND CURRENCY FRAGILITY
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages and persistent currency instability raise operating costs and increase reliance on external investors and cross-border infrastructure.
